m10-13-q1.s: In **DHCP starvation**, the attacker sends a flood of DHCPDISCOVERs from fake MAC addresses and **uses up every address in the pool**. Real users then can't get an IP address. Mitigate it with port security and DHCP snooping.
x: MAC flooding overflows the CAM table.

m10-13-q2.s: A MAC (CAM) table overflow happens when one port sends thousands of fake source MACs. **Port security** caps how many MACs a port can learn, which stops it.

m10-13-q3.s: Cisco's **endpoint** security products are the **Email Security Appliance (ESA)**, the **Web Security Appliance (WSA)** and the **NAC appliance**.
x: ASA, IPS sensors and VPN appliances protect the network perimeter, not endpoints.

m10-13-q4.s: **True.** In 802.1X the **supplicant** is the client asking for access. The **authenticator** is the switch or AP, and the **authentication server** is usually RADIUS.

m10-13-q5.s: **Local AAA** keeps usernames and passwords on the router itself. It's simple and fine for **small networks**. Server-based AAA (RADIUS or TACACS+) scales better.
code: R1(config)# aaa authentication login default local

m10-13-q6.s: CDP and LLDP reveal device models, IOS versions and addresses to anyone listening. **Disable them wherever they aren't needed**, especially on edge and user-facing ports.

m10-13-q7.s: Telnet sends everything, including passwords, in **plain text**. **SSH** encrypts the session.

m10-13-q8.s: When the CAM table is full, the switch can't learn new MAC addresses. It treats new frames as unknown unicasts and **floods them out every port in the same VLAN**, so an attacker can capture them. Flooding never leaves the VLAN.

m10-13-q9.s: The **supplicant** is the **client device** asking for access. The switch is the authenticator, and the RADIUS server is the authentication server.

m10-13-q10.s: To meet the goals you need: turn on port security, allow **2 MAC addresses** (phone + PC), and use **sticky** learning so the addresses are saved to the running configuration. The default violation mode, **shutdown**, already shuts the port, so no violation command is needed.
x: `violation restrict` would drop frames instead of shutting the port.
Without `switchport port-security` itself, nothing is enforced.

m10-13-q11.s: Fa0/12 allows only one manually set MAC address. PC1's MAC is different, so the default **shutdown** mode error-disables the port **immediately**, logs a message and increments the violation counter.

m10-13-q12.s: **Double-tagging** puts the attacker's frame in the **native VLAN** with a second, hidden tag. If the native VLAN is an **unused VLAN**, there's no user port in it to start the attack from.

m10-13-q13.s: `validate src-mac` makes DAI compare the **Ethernet source MAC** with the **sender MAC inside the ARP message**. If they differ, the ARP is dropped.
code: S1(config)# ip arp inspection validate src-mac
x: `dst-mac` compares the destination MAC with the ARP target MAC.

m10-13-q14.s: BPDU guard can be enabled **globally** for all PortFast ports, or **per interface**.

m10-13-q15.s: **Sticky** secure MAC addresses are learned dynamically but **written into the running configuration**. Once that configuration is saved, the addresses survive a reboot. Plain dynamic secure addresses are lost.

m10-13-q16.s: APs broadcast **beacons** regularly to announce the SSID and capabilities. Probe, authentication and association frames are only sent while a client is joining.

m10-13-q17.s: **Passive:** the client listens for the AP's **beacon** broadcasts. **Active:** the client sends a **probe request**, either for a specific SSID or for any.

m10-13-q18.s: In 2.4 GHz, channels **1, 6 and 11** don't overlap. Picking one of them **avoids interference** from nearby networks.

m10-13-q19.s: The SSID isn't broadcast (it's cloaked), so the AP doesn't appear in the list. Clients must already know the SSID and send probe requests, which the course calls the AP being in **active** mode.
x: In passive mode the AP broadcasts beacons, so the network would appear.
Mixed refers to supporting several 802.11 standards.

m10-13-q20.s: **802.11ac** (5 GHz) reaches about **1.3 Gb/s** and is backward compatible with a/n devices on 5 GHz. On a dual-band router, b/g/n devices still work too.

m10-13-q21.s: The first thing to do is **change the default admin username and password**, which are public knowledge. After that, set encryption (WPA2/WPA3), then other hardening.

m10-13-q22.s: The **Advanced** button on the 3504 WLC dashboard opens the full Summary page with every feature menu.

m10-13-q23.s: Each new WLAN on the WLC maps to its **own VLAN interface**, so you have to **create that interface first**.

m10-13-q24.s: **5 GHz** has many more non-overlapping channels and is **less crowded** than 2.4 GHz, so it carries streaming video better.
x: 5 GHz actually has *shorter* range than 2.4 GHz.

m10-13-q25.s: The **shared secret** is a password set on both the WLC and the RADIUS server. It **authenticates and encrypts the messages between them**. Users never type it.

m10-13-q26.s: Out of the box, change the **AP/admin password**, the **SSID** and the **wireless network password** (security key).
x: Antenna frequency and beacon timing don't need changing.
Client OS passwords have nothing to do with the AP.

m10-13-q27.s: **Authentication** checks *who you are*, typically with a username and password.

m10-13-q28.s: A **WLAN** (wireless LAN) uses the **802.11** standards on **2.4 or 5 GHz**.

m10-13-q29.s: **Port security** limits how many fake MAC addresses a port can use, and **DHCP snooping** rate-limits DHCP messages on untrusted ports. Together they stop DHCP starvation.
x: IP Source Guard stops IP and MAC spoofing.

m10-13-q30.s: VLAN hopping defenses: **set trunk ports manually**, **disable DTP** on all ports, and **move the native VLAN to an unused VLAN**. Also put unused ports in an unused VLAN and shut them down.

m10-13-q31.s: **Shutdown** is the **default violation mode** for any secure port. The output also shows a maximum of 2 MAC addresses with 1 learned (sticky), and the port is still up (no secure-shutdown).

m10-13-q32.s: **RADIUS** checks each user's credentials against a central server. That's WPA2/WPA3-**Enterprise** (802.1X).

m10-13-q33.s: Put the newer devices on **5 GHz** and leave the older b/g devices on **2.4 GHz**. Slow legacy clients then stop dragging everyone down. This is called splitting the traffic.

m10-13-q34.s: Microwave ovens run at about **2.4 GHz** and cause **accidental interference** that degrades the WLAN.

m10-13-q35.s: **CAPWAP** carries traffic between **lightweight APs and the WLC**: it encapsulates and forwards client traffic and control messages (UDP 5246/5247).
x: Over-the-air encryption is handled by WPA2/WPA3.

m10-13-q36.s: In the activity, Fa0/1 uses violation mode **protect**: frames from unknown MACs are **silently dropped**, with no syslog, no counter and no shutdown.

m10-13-q37.s:
**Authentication** – who are you? (username/password)
**Authorization** – what are you allowed to do?
**Accounting** – what did you do? (logs, usage)

m10-13-q38.s: AAA checks users against a central server using **RADIUS** (open standard, UDP) or **TACACS+** (Cisco, TCP 49).

m10-13-q39.s: DHCP starvation drains the pool, so **legitimate clients can't get an address**. It's a denial-of-service attack.
x: Handing clients false gateway or DNS information is *DHCP spoofing* (a rogue server).

m10-13-q40.s: Double-tagging only works when the attacker's access VLAN is **the same as the trunk's native VLAN**. That's why the native VLAN should be an unused VLAN.

m10-13-q41.s: **Accounting** records who accessed what, when, and which changes they made. It's the audit trail.

m10-13-q42.s: Trust every port **on the path toward the legitimate DHCP server**: AS3's port to the server (1), DS1 and DS2 toward AS3 (2), and the uplinks from AS1 and AS2 to DS1 and DS2 (4). **1 + 2 + 4 = 7**.

m10-13-q43.s: Unless you choose another mode, port security uses **shutdown**: the port is error-disabled on a violation.

m10-13-q44.s: Start with the simple checks: is the **wireless NIC turned on**, and is the **right SSID selected**?
x: The NIC picks the frequency automatically.

m10-13-q45.s: With **SSID cloaking**, clients have to **type the SSID manually** to connect. It's weak security, though: the SSID still shows up in probe and association frames.
x: Real protection comes from encryption and authentication (WPA2/WPA3).

m10-13-q46.s: **Enterprise** mode (WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise) authenticates each user through **802.1X and a RADIUS server**. Personal mode uses one shared passphrase.

m10-13-q47.s: **Split the traffic** between the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands, for example with separate SSIDs, so the load is spread out and time-sensitive traffic gets the cleaner 5 GHz band.

m10-13-q48.s: **SNMP** is used to monitor and manage network devices: counters, traps and status.

m10-13-q49.s: 10.0.10.0/24 is a **private** network that can't be routed on the internet. The wireless router uses **NAT** (PAT) to translate those addresses to its public IP.

m10-13-q50.s: **QoS** prioritizes time-sensitive traffic, like voice and video, over email and web browsing.

m10-13-q51.s: **802.1X** defines three roles: the **supplicant** (client), the **authenticator** (switch or AP) and the **authentication server** (RADIUS).

m10-13-q52.s: A **WWAN** (wireless WAN), such as a cellular or satellite network, covers **national or global** areas.

m10-13-q53.s: Basic VLAN hopping abuses **DTP**: by default a port can be talked into trunking, and then the attacker sees every VLAN. Fix it with access mode plus `switchport nonegotiate`.

m10-13-q54.s: **Authorization** decides **what an authenticated user may access and do**.

m10-13-q55.s: The violation counter is 1, and the port allows only one manually set MAC. **PC1's MAC doesn't match 0023.189d.6456**, so the port shut down (the default mode).
x: PC-to-switch connections use straight-through cables, so the cable isn't the problem.

m10-13-q56.s: `ip dhcp snooping limit rate 6` lets each of ports Fa0/5–10 receive **up to 6 DHCP messages per second**. Extra messages are dropped (on many platforms the port can also be error-disabled).
code: SW1(config-if-range)# ip dhcp snooping limit rate 6

m10-13-q57.s: **protect** silently drops frames from unknown MACs: **no syslog, no SNMP trap, no counter**. restrict drops *and* notifies; shutdown error-disables the port.

m10-13-q58.s: Dual-band routers use the same SSID on both bands by default. **Giving each band its own SSID** is the simplest way to split the traffic.

m10-13-q59.s: **Authorization** controls what users can do once they're logged in.

m10-13-q60.s: A **WMAN** (wireless metropolitan-area network) covers a **city or district**.

m10-13-q61.s: The **WLANs** tab is where you create and edit WLANs, including security settings such as WPA2, QoS and policies.

m10-13-q62.s: **Omnidirectional** antennas radiate in all directions (360°), which suits hallways and large open rooms. Yagi, dish and other directional antennas focus the signal in one direction.

m10-13-q64.s: BPDU guard **error-disables a PortFast (edge) port as soon as it receives a BPDU**. That stops anyone from plugging in a **rogue switch**.

m10-13-q65.s: **Accounting** can log every EXEC and configuration command a user enters.

m10-13-q66.s: A **WWAN** uses transmitters to cover very large geographic areas, as cellular networks do.

m10-13-q67.s: **Authentication** decides **who** is allowed onto the network.

m10-13-q69.s: A **WPAN** (wireless personal-area network) uses low-power, short-range links of about **6–9 m**, such as Bluetooth.

m10-13-q70.s: **Infrastructure** mode uses access points that connect clients to the wired network. That's how a whole building gets coverage.
x: A hotspot is a device sharing its connection.
Mixed mode is about supporting several standards.

m10-13-q71.s: A **WMAN** provides wireless service across a large **urban** area.

m10-13-q73.s: For each service a client requests, **authorization** answers with **PASS or FAIL**: is it allowed or not.

m10-13-q74.s: **WMANs** often use antennas or devices **mounted on buildings** to cover a city.

m10-13-q75.s: `ip arp inspection validate src-mac` checks that the **Ethernet source MAC matches the ARP sender MAC**.
code: S1(config)# ip arp inspection validate src-mac

m10-13-q76.s: **Accounting** collects and reports **usage data**, such as session time and bytes, for billing and auditing.

m10-13-q77.s: A **WLAN** covers a medium-sized area, up to about **300 ft (91 m)**.

m10-13-q78.s: **Accounting** audits what users actually did on the network.

m10-13-q79.s: **Bluetooth** and **ZigBee** are **WPAN** technologies: short range and low power.

m10-13-q80.s: **Authentication** can be done **locally** (usernames stored on the device) or **server-based** (RADIUS or TACACS+).

m10-13-q81.s: To split the traffic, give each band a **different SSID**, then use **5 GHz for streaming and time-sensitive traffic** and **2.4 GHz for basic browsing and email**.
x: The split works by band, not by security mode, and a shared SSID defeats it.

m10-13-q82.s: **802.1X** (port-based access control) keeps publicly reachable switch ports closed until the user authenticates.
